nameStory: The 'Hoof Fungus' gets its name from its distinctive shape that looks remarkably like a horse's hoof attached to a tree trunk. It's also called the 'Ice Man Fungus' because the famous 5,000-year-old mummy Ötzi was found carrying four pieces of this fungus in his pouch. He likely used it as tinder to start fires during his mountain travels.
description: Hoof Fungus is a large, perennial bracket fungus that grows directly from the sides of hardwood tree trunks without a stem. These woody shelf-like growths can persist for years, slowly expanding in size as they develop distinctive hoof-shaped profiles. The fruiting bodies are tough and woody, ranging from silvery-gray to dark brown or nearly black, and can grow quite large over time. This species creates white rot in the wood it colonizes, breaking down the tree's structure.

idTips.label: Shape
idTips.description: Distinctive hoof or bracket shape jutting out from tree trunks, with a rounded, bulbous profile that's wider at the bottom than where it attaches to the tree

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Hard, woody exterior that feels like touching a piece of weathered wood or stone, often with concentric ridges and a smooth to slightly cracked surface

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Variable coloring from silvery-gray when young to brown, dark brown, or nearly black with age, often showing different colored zones

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Underneath surface has tiny, round pores (not gills) that are cream to brown colored and feel firm to the touch

idTips.label: Attachment
idTips.description: Grows directly from tree trunk with no visible stem, firmly attached and very difficult to remove without tools

idTips.label: Durability
idTips.description: Extremely hard and persistent, remaining on trees for multiple years and surviving harsh weather conditions

habitat: Found growing on the trunks of various hardwood trees throughout New England's forests, particularly on birch, beech, maple, and oak. Look for them in both deciduous and mixed forests from lowland areas to mountain slopes. They typically appear on dead or dying trees but can also be found on apparently healthy trees where they exist as hidden internal fungi.

seasonality.spring: Existing fruiting bodies are easily spotted as leaves emerge, and you may notice new growth starting as white margins on established brackets. Spring rains can cause the pores to release spores.
seasonality.summer: Established fruiting bodies continue growing slowly and are highly visible. This is an excellent time to observe their firm texture and examine the pore surface underneath.
seasonality.fall: Peak time for spotting these fungi as deciduous leaves drop and reveal brackets clearly on bare trunks. Mature specimens are at their most distinctive size and coloring.
seasonality.winter: Persistent fruiting bodies remain clearly visible on snow-covered trees, making them one of the easiest fungi to find and study during cold months when most other fungi are dormant.

funFact: This fungus was so valuable for starting fires that Ötzi the Iceman carried it in his survival kit 5,000 years ago, and it was processed into 'amadou' - a feltlike material that could catch the tiniest spark and was used by our ancestors long before matches were invented!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large bracket fungi, but Hoof Fungus is distinguished by its characteristic bulbous, hoof-like profile and extremely hard texture. Remember: if it looks like a horse's hoof stuck to a tree and feels rock-hard, you've likely found the right species.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'false tinder fungus' in some regions, this species actually makes excellent tinder and the 'false' designation comes from European naming conventions distinguishing it from other tinder-producing fungi. The term 'amadou' comes from French and refers to the processed inner material that becomes incredibly flammable.
compareHints: Unlike its relative the Tinder Polypore (Fomes excavatus), Hoof Fungus has a more pronounced bulbous shape rather than a flatter bracket form. Sweet Knot (Fomes graveolens) typically has a more irregular, knobby appearance and different coloration patterns. Hoof Fungus is generally the largest and most hoof-shaped of the Fomes species in New England.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative Hoof Fungus, Tinder Polypore has a much darker, more blackened upper surface and tends to be significantly harder to the touch.
